appraisal_events.evidence: « il l'avait rencontrée, il lui avait trouvé mauvais genre » ; « Qu'avait-il voulu dire par mauvais genre ? [...] peut-être avait-il voulu dire genre gomorrhéen » ; « cette odieuse Albertine ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Aimé's remembered verdict that Albertine has 'mauvais genre' locally discredits her, and the narrator's jealousy escalates it into a suspicion of Gomorrah and the epithet 'odieuse'. The passage ironizes rather than endorses this appraisal: it leaves the phrase undecidable between 'vulgaire' and 'gomorrhéen', and its own maxim states that the jealous man forms 'des soupçons atroces à propos de faits innocents'.

appraisal_events.evidence: « ma pensée, qui jusqu'ici avait navigué en souriant sur ces eaux bienheureuses, éclatait soudain, comme si elle eût heurté une mine invisible » ; « J'avais beau questionner, c'était moi qui répondais, je n'apprenais rien de plus » ; « il faudrait que j'écrive à Aimé [...] je demandai à celui-ci [Bloch] [...] de me montrer seulement une photographie d'elle ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's own retrospective analysis stages his collapse from luminous reverie into a jealousy he cannot resolve: split in two, he interrogates himself and learns nothing, and ends dependent on Aimé's words and on a humiliating request to Bloch. The essayistic frame ('l'amour est un mal inguérissable') makes this diminishment narrator-endorsed rather than merely reported.

status_effects.explanation: The dominant local movement carries him from beatific possession ('Combien je possédais plus Albertine aujourd'hui !') into an unappeasable jealous attack whose future appears 'atroce'; the early uplift is explicitly detonated mid-passage rather than sustained.

He loses all epistemic authority within the passage: his self-questioning yields nothing, and he must solicit Aimé and Bloch for the knowledge he cannot produce, even manufacturing uncertainty to blunt his own pain.

She is locally lowered by Aimé's dismissive verdict and by the narrator's recoil ('cette odieuse Albertine'), though the fall is softened because the passage marks the charge as jealous conjecture rather than established fact.
Two words of his govern the whole passage: he is the sole source of knowledge about Albertine, and the narrator plans to write to him and seek him out to have them interpreted.

ambiguities: The passage deliberately leaves 'mauvais genre' undecided between 'genre vulgaire' and 'genre gomorrhéen', so the severity and even the kind of discredit attaching to Albertine is unfixed by the text itself.

Narrator stance toward the jealous appraisal is layered: the free indirect jealousy ('cette odieuse Albertine') is framed by an essayistic maxim that treats such suspicions as self-administered and directed at 'faits innocents', which argues for an ironized rather than endorsed reading of E1.

The opening reverie contains a genuine positive note ('Combien je possédais plus Albertine aujourd'hui !'), but it is placed early and explicitly exploded, so it is read as a qualifying counter-movement rather than the dominant outcome.
